title: What Should CS Students Learn in the AI Era?
note: One English line per Korean source line; timing comes from the Korean performance. No English TTS.

scenes.title: You sat down to study, not rethink your entire career
lines: Picture a day like this. You sit down to solve a coding interview problem and polish your portfolio. Then you open a video with this title: Developers are finished.
One side says you will fall behind without AI. The other says using AI stops you from learning. So should I turn it on or off? I came here to study, and now I am questioning my entire career.

You have not even started your first job, and people are already declaring it extinct. That is hard to laugh off. Everyone else seems to be building things, while you are still stuck setting up your environment. It can feel like you alone are falling behind.
Today, I will do more than tell you not to worry. Let us look at what helps AI-assisted work become a skill you actually own, from exams and interviews to your first job.

scenes.title: Does everyone at the company know what they are doing?
lines: At this point, you might think: surely people already working at companies know what I should prepare for? Let us step into an imaginary meeting room.

The boss says, Can AI do all of this? An executive asks, Does that halve the cost? The team lead concludes, Great, let us halve the schedule too. Nobody has reviewed the code, but the deadline has already been optimized.

That is a little exaggerated. But a senior job title does not automatically mean understanding a technology's capabilities and limits. Working once in a demo is not the same as working reliably in our service.

That leaves job seekers frustrated. You are expected to use AI well and have solid fundamentals. So separate your goals. Leave yourself time to think through what you are learning, and get help with repetitive work you already understand. Always follow the tool-use rules for assignments and exams.

scenes.title: You asked for a fix. Something else broke.
lines: You paste in an error: Fix this. You try the suggested code, and a different error appears. Fix this too. Eventually, it runs. But you cannot explain what changed.
When you are in a hurry, getting it to run is a relief. But if the same problem comes back tomorrow, you may have to start that conversation all over again.

Pick one error and investigate it. If a loop should run five times but only runs four, write down the expected result. Set a breakpoint and follow the variables. Find the point where reality stops matching your expectations.

Fix the condition and check the same input again. Read documentation or ask for a hint if you get stuck. The important part is not how many hours you struggled alone. It is whether you can later explain the mistake in one sentence.

scenes.title: Fundamentals matter. But when do I study all of them?
lines: Fundamentals matter. That is true. But the list includes data structures, algorithms, operating systems, networking, and databases. I came to prepare for a job, not enroll in another degree.

You do not have to finish all of those subjects before building anything. Start with one question about your current feature. How should requests be handled in the order they arrive? How should data be found by name?
A queue might address the first question, and a dictionary the second. Explore what changes as the data grows. Fundamentals stop being a memorization checklist and become reasons for your decisions.

The same goes for networking and databases. Trace where a request failed or why the stored value differs, and learn the concepts you need along the way. Instead of mastering every subject at once, start with one part of your project you cannot explain.

scenes.title: Nice portfolio. Why did you choose this technology?
lines: When you build a portfolio, it is tempting to add one more technology. Everyone else's project looks impressive. Soon, your little notes app has several servers and a cache. You wanted a notepad and nearly built a data center.
Now imagine an interviewer asks: Why did you design it this way? If your entire answer is, AI recommended it, your own judgment is hard to see.

You do not need a grand explanation. I kept the setup small because it is a single-user program. I separated the processing because concurrent edits were possible. Start with specific reasons like those.

What matters is not using fewer technologies for its own sake, but knowing why you chose them. Trace the path from input to processing to output in your own words. Wherever your explanation stalls is a good place to study next.

scenes.title: Why does the first line disappear in an interview?
lines: You definitely built it at home. It ran, and reading the code made sense. Then an exam or interview asks you to implement it without help. On paper or in an editor, suddenly you cannot even write the first line.

You can picture the finished screen, but your hands stop at the function name. Nerves and time pressure matter too. Getting stuck once does not mean you have no ability. But recognizing an answer and planning the steps from scratch need separate practice.

Suppose you must remove duplicate names while keeping the order of their first appearance. Before writing code, write a small input and the output you want. Decide where to remember names you have seen and where to put new ones.
Then turn those plain-language steps into loops and conditions. If you get stuck, ask AI for just the next condition to check, not the entire solution.
Once you solve it, close the answer and try a small variation with different input. Rather than memorizing one problem, practice how to start from a blank page.

scenes.title: A small game is not always a small job
lines: If you want to build something yourself, a small game like Tetris is a good option. Just drop a few blocks, right? That is an easy assumption to make. But while the blocks fall, your to-do list keeps stacking up.

Store the board in a two-dimensional array and represent a four-cell piece with coordinates. It moves down over time, and key presses move it sideways or rotate it. You also have to check whether the next position overlaps a wall or another block.

When it cannot move farther down, lock it into the board. Remove completed rows and move the rows above them down. Decide what happens when rotation is blocked near a wall, and when the game ends if a new piece cannot spawn. If you do not define the rules, your bugs will do it for you.

Building Tetris does not guarantee you a job. It is practice connecting input, data, collision checks, and state changes into something finished. Before adding more features to a huge unfinished project, complete something small that you can explain yourself.

scenes.title: Why would you press that? That is testing.
lines: It works now. You show a friend, and they immediately shove a piece against the wall and hammer the rotate button. Why would you rotate it there? Well, my program is the one that lets them press that button.

If you have only dropped one piece in the middle, try other conditions. What if two rows fill at once? What if a piece rotates next to stacked blocks? What if there is nowhere for a new piece to spawn? What if keys are pressed after game over? The rules must hold outside your favorite demo.

Write the expected result and compare it with what happens. Reject rotations through a wall. Clear only the completed rows, together. Keep problem inputs as tests, so you can see whether a later change breaks the same behavior again.
Passing tests does not mean every problem is gone. But you can add specific checked conditions to the claim that it works. You can also ask AI to suggest edge cases you may have missed.

scenes.title: The AI bill arrives before your first paycheck
lines: Job seekers face another practical problem. You already pay for courses and living expenses. If every useful tool needs another payment, that adds up. Your developer-tool subscriptions start work before your salary does.

Models such as Astra and Claude Fable also require attention to usage costs. The on-screen prices are standard API usage rates checked in September 2026. They are not monthly subscription fees. Input and output are billed separately using units of text called tokens.

Your actual bill depends on usage, retries, and discounts for reusing the same content. Even a higher unit price can mean lower cost per task if fewer attempts are needed. Do not judge only by expensive or cheap. Look at the whole job.
Prices could rise, or free allowances could shrink. That is not a prediction that they definitely will. The point is to keep a way to continue working if today's terms change.

Performance deserves the same approach. Test supposedly faster code with the same input, and compare both time and results. This is not advice to buy the most expensive tool. Choose the help you need and expand what you can verify yourself.

scenes.title: Almost done. So why is the task still open?
lines: Now imagine you have started your first job. Your feature works on screen. You tell your team lead, Almost done. But empty input causes an error, a failed save freezes the screen, and integrating another feature breaks it again.
The next day, it is still almost done. The feature moves, but the task is going nowhere. There was a gap between building the visible screen and finishing the work you were assigned.
Delays are not always a junior developer's fault. Requirements change, schedules are tight, or nobody is available to review the work. Before struggling alone, agree on what counts as done.

Write down whether valid input alone is enough, what message should appear on failure, whether saved values are correct, and whether integration works. Include the necessary checks for secrets, permissions, and the suitability of new libraries.
You can report progress differently too. Valid input works; save-error handling is still pending. I have checked these parts, and I would like help reviewing this condition.

Put AI-generated code through the team's tests and review process as well. This does not mean a junior developer carries all the responsibility. Making progress and blockers visible helps other people give you specific support.

scenes.title: Easy for you to say. You already have a job.
lines: A senior developer says, I can build it from scratch without AI. A job seeker might think: You already have a job. Right now, I just need to get my foot in the door.

That is fair. Different starting points mean we cannot demand that everyone spend their time the same way. The useful lesson is not a senior developer's story of suffering. It is the experience of starting from an empty file. Age alone does not give you that experience.

You do not need to declare that you will build everything yourself. Choose just one feature: save a line of notes, or move a Tetris piece one cell. Turn off AI autocomplete briefly and decide for yourself where to begin.

If you prepare the runtime, required libraries, and documentation in advance, you can build and run local programs like these without internet access. Features that require an external server or a new download are a separate matter.

Get help when you need it. Then close the answer and start again. Compare your own version with the AI-assisted version, and record what you learned and fixed. Move from being unable to work without the tool to being able to begin, even slowly.

scenes.title: The small thing you finished stays with you
lines: Getting stuck in one exam, receiving a disappointing application result, or delivering one task late does not erase everything you have learned. But hearing that things will be fine does not instantly make the worry disappear either.
I cannot give you the answer to which tools will appear or how hiring will change. But if you can fix an error today that you could not explain yesterday, that is a real change you keep.
Do not make today's plan too big. Take one small input, process it, check the result, and finish. Practice explaining that sequence in interviews and describing what remains to your team.

The goal is not to become someone who never uses AI. It is to keep your own judgment when you use it, and still be able to start when you cannot. Fundamentals and tool skills do not require you to abandon one for the other.

Set the AI hype aside for a moment and choose one feature to finish with your own hands today. Faster with AI, but not helpless without it. Subscribe to tools if you want. Just do not make your skills subscription-only.
